sources.title: Joaquín Torres-García (Q520713), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Joaquín Torres-García', description 'Spanish Uruguayan painter, sculptor, writer and theorist of modern art (1874-1949)', instance of human, born 1874-07-28, died 1949-08-08, citizen of Uruguay and Spain; no Korean label and no Korean Wikipedia article. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Joaquín Torres-García' (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him the Uruguayan painter who introduced Constructivism to South America; he studied at Barcelona's Academy of Fine Arts from 1894, worked in a modern Classicism for about 16 years, went to New York in 1920, returned to Europe in 1922 and came to know the Constructivist ideas of Mondrian and Van Doesburg, took part in the Cercle et Carré group, evolved a grid filled with symbols, returned to Montevideo in 1934, founded the Association of Constructivist Art in 1935 with the lecture 'The School of the South', built the stone-and-cement Cosmic Monument (1938) and founded the Taller Torres-García in 1943, whose influence on Uruguayan and Argentine art lasted a generation. Short reference article, admiring in tone.

Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, biography of Joaquín Torres-García by Dominique Lora (read in full): early training in Barcelona, illustrations and stained-glass work with Gaudí's circle in Palma Cathedral and the Sagrada Familia (1903-04), the 1912 commission for the Saló Sant Jordi frescoes that sparked critical debate, the Escola de Decoració at Terrassa, the 1920 move to New York where he designed toys, meeting Mondrian in Paris in 1928 and founding Cercle et Carré, the 1934 return to Uruguay and the Asociación de Arte Constructivo and Taller Torres-García, the Cosmic Monument (1938) and the 1944 book Universalismo constructivo. Museum biography; chronology-level and admiring.

Ana María Franco, 'Joaquín Torres García's Constructive Universalism', Ensayos: Historia y Teoría del Arte no. 10 (Universidad Nacional de Colombia, 2005), pp. 102-141 (peer-reviewed art-history article, read in full from the Dialnet PDF). SUBSTANTIVE BEHAVIOURAL SOURCE with a counter-voice: he arrived in Paris in 1926 aged 52 and practically unknown; he and Hélion organised the 1928 'Cinq Refusés' exhibition after the Salon d'Automne rejected them; he declined to join Van Doesburg's all-abstract Art Concret group because he held that wholly abstract art was incomplete, co-founded Cercle et Carré with Seuphor in 1930 (administrative duties) and resigned in July 1930 when Seuphor altered one of his texts on figuration; friends read his figurative commitment as indecision and some critics called him eclectic, while the author argues the tension produced an original programme; his 1934 return to Montevideo, almost weekly lectures, the 1935 Asociación de Arte Constructivo, the 1936 magazine Círculo y Cuadrado, the Taller Torres-García (dated 1944 here, 1943 in other sources). Relies partly on his own autobiography Historia de mi vida.

Geaninne Gutiérrez-Guimarães, 'Spirit of America: Joaquín Torres-García in New York, 1920-1922', Parts 1 and 2, MoMA post (Museum of Modern Art, essay from the catalogue of the 2011 Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya exhibition; both parts read). Curatorial scholarship drawing on his letters, his unpublished manuscript 'New York' and Historia de mi vida: he left Barcelona in 1920 with his wife and three children after officials forced him to abandon the Saló Sant Jordi fresco commission, saying he would make wooden toys; he met Katherine Dreier and the Société Anonyme and sold works; the toy firms Artist Toy Makers (1921) and Aladdin Toy Company (1924) did not succeed, and in July 1922 he left New York to return to painting, blaming himself for 'that hateful commercial thing'; later his Asociación de Arte Constructivo linked constructivism to pre-Columbian art.

Karen Grimson, 'Joaquín Torres-García's Creative Paradox', MoMA Inside/Out blog, 13 January 2016 (read): notes that after returning to Uruguay in 1934 at age 60 he founded and directed the Asociación de Arte Constructivo (signed AAC on his paintings of 1935-38), that the black-and-white structure paintings of those years are among the most striking synthetic abstraction made in the Americas, and that his modernising vision was rooted in antiquity and the ancestral. Museum blog; used for achievement context only, not for any scored row.

Encyclopedia.com reference entry 'Torres García, Joaquín (1874-1949)' (read): founding member of Cercle et Carré (1930) and the Asociación de Arte Constructivo (1935), murals and the stained-glass windows of Palma Cathedral, his books Structure (1935), The Tradition of Abstract Man (1938), The Metaphysics of Indo-American Prehistory (1940) and Universal Constructivism (1944); gives his birth date as 25 July where other sources give 28 July. Short reference entry, used only for consistent facts.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_tg_franco, src_tg_britannica, src_tg_thyssen | 1926-1944 | scholarly article, reference biography, museum biography] Franco documents that in Paris he took only what was useful to him from Cubism, Neoplasticism and primitive art and combined it with figurative symbols in a golden-section grid, a programme she calls original; Britannica and the Thyssen biography record the resulting grid of symbols and the pre-Columbian turn. The same article reports contemporaries and some critics calling him eclectic and not personally original, so the claim is a critical judgement rather than a measured behaviour; lowered during calibration.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_tg_thyssen, src_tg_britannica, src_tg_moma_ny, src_tg_encyclopedia | 1893-1944 | museum biography, reference biography, curatorial essay, reference entry] Four sources independently list sustained work in several media and roles: illustration for periodicals, murals and frescoes, stained glass, easel painting, stone-and-cement monuments, wooden toys marketed to firms in several countries, teaching and written theory. Breadth is documented across sources; depth in each field is not scored.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_tg_franco, src_tg_britannica, src_tg_encyclopedia | 1930-1944 | scholarly article, reference biography, reference entry] He wrote a doctrine of structure and construction (Estructura 1935, Universalismo constructivo 1944) and built paintings on a golden-section grid divided into compartments of symbols; Franco quotes his texts calling geometric art universal and resting on a law of unity. Most of the evidence about the doctrine is his own writing as read by one scholar, so the row is moderate; lowered during calibration.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_tg_franco, src_tg_thyssen, src_tg_britannica, src_tg_moma_ny | 1913-1944 | scholarly article, museum biography, reference biography, curatorial essay] Distinct episodes of starting things rather than waiting for institutions are documented across sources: the Escola de Decoració at Terrassa, the 1928 counter-exhibition with Hélion after the Salon d'Automne refused them, the 1930 Cercle et Carré group and magazine, and in Montevideo the 1935 Asociación de Arte Constructivo, its 1936 magazine and the Taller. The Paris and Montevideo episodes lean on Franco; the Terrassa school and the Taller rest on the museum and reference biographies; lowered slightly during calibration.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_tg_franco, src_tg_britannica, src_tg_moma_ny | 1934-1944 | scholarly article, reference biography, curatorial essay] After returning at 60 he gave almost weekly lectures, wrote a textbook for the Asociación's students, launched a magazine and taught at the Taller, with the stated aim of a 'School of the South'; Franco quotes a scholar saying he felt and said he had a mission to open America to contemporary aesthetics. The mission language is largely his own and its retelling, so this is a lean toward purpose-driven work rather than a strong score; lowered during calibration.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_tg_franco | 1929-1930 | scholarly article] Franco reports that he refused to sign Van Doesburg's manifesto for an all-abstract group because he thought wholly abstract art incomplete, then resigned from Cercle et Carré in July 1930 when Seuphor changed his text on figuration; close friends read the same stance as indecision. Both episodes come from one scholarly account built on the participants' memoirs, so concentration was high; lowered to an inference-level lean during calibration.

adaptability.rationale: [src_tg_franco, src_tg_moma_ny, src_tg_britannica | 1916-1934 | scholarly article, curatorial essay, reference biography] He changed country and manner several times (Barcelona classicism, a Cubist-Futurist phase from 1916, New York in 1920, Paris from 1926 where he 'acclimatised', Madrid, then Montevideo in 1934) and left New York in 1922 when the toy venture failed. Several moves were forced by circumstance and Franco stresses that his ideas about art evolved without abrupt change, so the row is a modest inference; lowered during calibration.

persistence.rationale: [src_tg_franco, src_tg_moma_ny | 1920-1930 | scholarly article, curatorial essay] Franco notes his first Paris show in 1926 made little impact and the 1928 Salon rejected him, yet he stayed and developed his programme; the New York essay records job rejections and the failed toy venture before he returned to painting. Both accounts draw on his autobiography and letters, so they are one family of self-report; lowered to an inference-level lean during calibration.

portrait.reason: No lifetime likeness could be shipped with clean holder terms and a verified sitter. (1) Ramon Casas charcoal drawing c. 1901 (MNAC 027317-D): the item record says 'Domini public' for the work, but the museum's legal notice licenses its site images CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 with a separate rates sheet for digital images, and the museum's own Europeana record for the item states CC BY-NC 4.0; the holder's terms therefore restrict non-commercial-only reuse of the digital image and conflict with the Commons PD tag; the drawing is also a full-length figure with a very small face. (2) Girona municipal photograph (Europeana, Ajuntament de Girona item 352075, 'Portrait of Joaquim Torres Garcia painting', 1920-1930, Public Domain Mark): sitter identification rests only on the catalogue heading, the photographer and original publication are unknown, the scan is a halftone reproduction, and the holder's item page and reuse terms could not be read (HTTP 403 / no terms page found). (3) Commons 1903 Sagrada Familia photograph: undocumented publication chain. Not substituting another person; no bot wall bypassed.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / lead did NOT survive: the MNAC Casas drawing is public domain by creator death (Casas d. 1932) and the holder item field says public domain, but the holder's legal notice (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 for site images, rates for digital images) and the holder-supplied Europeana record (CC BY-NC 4.0) restrict the digital image and the drawing is a full-length figure; the Girona photograph was found as a replacement lead but sitter, creator, first publication and holder terms are not verifiable. Portrait HELD; evidence otherwise complete. QID VERIFIED LIVE 2026-11-24 (Q520713, human, 1874-1949). REGION latin_america (born Montevideo, programme and school in Uruguay; lived 43 years in Europe). ZERO POLITICS. Korean name is a transliteration (no Korean Wikipedia article or Wikidata Korean label found). Caveats: Taller founding date differs by source (1943 Britannica and Thyssen, 1944 Franco); Encyclopedia.com gives 25 July as birth date against 28 July elsewhere; Franco and the MoMA essay both lean on his autobiography Historia de mi vida; sparse profile (8 scored rows) by design, not padded.
